title: "Performance and Zero-Cost Abstractions"

# Performance and Zero-Cost Abstractions

An iterator chain of simple arithmetic is allowed to compile to the same loop you would have written by hand. That is a property of the optimizer in release mode, not a property of debug builds, and not a property of chains that allocate a `String` per item.

## The concept

In `--release`, `map` and `filter` on integers are usually inlined. What remains is a loop and the work you actually asked for. The costs that survive are the ones in the closures: allocation, a virtual call, a lock, I/O, or a `collect` you did not need.

Debug builds do not inline this aggressively. Do not time iterators with `cargo run`. Time `cargo run --release`, and pass outputs through `std::hint::black_box` so the compiler cannot delete the loop.

## Recipe 49 — Verifying zero-cost with a benchmark

Sum `n * 2` for `0..LEN` with a chain and with a `for` loop. On a release build the two times should be in the same band. A debug build is not the comparison.

```rust
use std::hint::black_box;
use std::time::Instant;

fn by_iter(data: &[i64]) -> i64 {
    data.iter().map(|n| n * 2).sum()
}

fn by_loop(data: &[i64]) -> i64 {
    let mut total = 0i64;
    for n in data {
        total += n * 2;
    }
    total
}

fn time(label: &str, data: &[i64], f: fn(&[i64]) -> i64) -> i64 {
    let start = Instant::now();
    let total = f(data);
    let elapsed = start.elapsed();
    black_box(total);
    println!("{label}: {elapsed:?} total={total}");
    total
}

fn main() {
    let len = black_box(5_000_000usize);
    let data: Vec<i64> = (0..len as i64).collect();
    let data = black_box(data);
    let a = time("iter", &data, by_iter);
    let b = time("loop", &data, by_loop);
    assert_eq!(a, b);
}
```

`black_box` on the length and on the `Vec` stops the compiler from treating the sum as a constant and deleting the loop. Compile with `rustc -O --edition 2024`. One release run on the machine that checked this chapter (rustc 1.98, x86-64) took about 2.5 ms for the iterator and about 2.4 ms for the loop, with the same total `24999995000000`. Your numbers will differ. If the iterator side is far slower, you are not in a release build, or the closure does something the loop does not.

## Recipe 50 — Avoiding intermediate allocations

This version builds a `Vec` of doubled values and then sums it. The `Vec` is pure overhead.

```rust
fn main() {
    let readings = [1, 2, 3, 4];
    let doubled: Vec<_> = readings.iter().map(|n| n * 2).collect();
    let total: i32 = doubled.iter().sum();
    assert_eq!(total, 20);

    let direct: i32 = readings.iter().map(|n| n * 2).sum();
    assert_eq!(direct, 20);
}
```

`sum` is the consumer. It does not need the doubled values stored. The same applies to `any`, `all`, `find`, and `fold`. Collect when the caller needs the collection later. Do not collect just to call one method that iterators already have.

## Recipe 51 — Choosing between iterator chains and for loops for performance

For straight-line arithmetic, choose the form you can read. Release codegen is usually the same loop. Choose the `for` loop when you measured a difference, or when the body has several early exits.

The recipe 49 program is the measurement. If you add a `filter` that the `for` loop also has, keep the comparison fair: same items, same `black_box`, release mode, more than one run. A single `Instant` sample is a smoke test, not a benchmark suite. Criterion is the tool when the difference is a few percent and you need to defend it.

## Recipe 52 — When collect() is expensive and what to do instead

`collect::<Vec<String>>()` allocates once per string plus the vector growth. If the next step joins them, build one `String`.

```rust
fn main() {
    let names = ["ada", "linus", "grace"];

    let owned: Vec<String> = names.iter().map(|name| name.to_uppercase()).collect();
    let joined_from_vec = owned.join(",");

    let mut direct = String::new();
    for (index, name) in names.iter().enumerate() {
        if index > 0 {
            direct.push(',');
        }
        direct.extend(name.chars().flat_map(|ch| ch.to_uppercase()));
    }

    assert_eq!(joined_from_vec, "ADA,LINUS,GRACE");
    assert_eq!(direct, "ADA,LINUS,GRACE");
}
```

The second form never stores the three uppercased strings. `char::to_uppercase` yields an iterator of `char` because some characters expand to more than one. `extend` writes them into the one buffer.

If you do need the `Vec`, and you know the length, `Vec::with_capacity` plus a loop, or an iterator whose `size_hint` lower bound is exact, avoids geometric reallocations of the vector itself. It does not remove the per-string allocations.

## Recipe 53 — Exploiting SIMD via iterator chains

Portable SIMD lives in `std::simd` and is not a stable API on the toolchain this book uses. What is stable is ordinary arithmetic that LLVM can autovectorize.

The shape that vectorizes is a tight loop over a slice of primitive numbers, with no allocation, no `unwrap` that can panic on a per-element basis the compiler must treat as a side exit, and no opaque function call it cannot inline. A chain does that:

```rust
fn scale_in_place(samples: &mut [f32]) {
    for sample in samples.iter_mut() {
        *sample *= 0.5;
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut samples = [1.0f32, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0];
    scale_in_place(&mut samples);
    assert_eq!(samples, [0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0]);
}
```

`samples.iter_mut().for_each(|sample| *sample *= 0.5)` is the same loop after inlining. Inspect the assembly with `rustc -O --edition 2024 --emit asm` if you need to see vector instructions on your target. Do not promise SIMD in a comment because a chain "looks functional". A `map` that formats a `String` will not vectorize. The memory traffic is the strings.

## Recipe 54 — Profiling an iterator pipeline

Time the whole consumer first. If it is hot, split the chain so you can see which closure is the cost.

```rust
fn main() {
    use std::hint::black_box;
    use std::time::Instant;

    let readings: Vec<i32> = (0..200_000).collect();
    let start = Instant::now();
    let total: i64 = readings
        .iter()
        .filter(|n| *n % 3 == 0)
        .map(|n| i64::from(*n) * i64::from(*n))
        .sum();
    let elapsed = start.elapsed();
    black_box(total);
    println!("pipeline {elapsed:?} total={total}");
    assert!(total > 0);
}
```

When the number matters, build with debug symbols in release (`-C debuginfo=1`) and sample with `perf record -g` or `cargo flamegraph` on the binary. In the profile, time inside your closure is your algorithm. Time in `alloc` is a `collect` or a `String`. Time in `Iterator::next` that does not inline means the closure was not visible to the compiler: it was a function pointer, a trait object, or you profiled a debug build.

A pipeline that is fast and unreadable is still the wrong pipeline. Measure, then decide whether the `for` loop in the next chapters is the one you ship.
